title: Visarjan: the god who stays
hookLine: Ganesha carried to the water, a boy's pillar remembered, and why nothing is lost when the clay goes under
carry: visarjan: god stays when the clay goes

lines: A RIVER OF PEOPLE TO THE SEA.
cards: It's the last day. The Ganesha who's been sitting in the living room, fed and sung to, is lifted off his seat for one last arti.

Then out the door, into a street that's become a river of people: drums, dancing, Ganesha after Ganesha moving slowly toward the sea. At the shore, people wade in and lower him into the water. He slips under.
And the whole beach shouts: Ganpati Bappa Morya, pudhchya varshi lavkar ya. Father Ganesha, come early next year. A lot of people are crying.

teach.b: The immersion is called visarjan, from a Sanskrit root meaning to let go, to release.
It happens on different days in different homes: after a day and a half, or three, five, seven, and the biggest crowds on Anant Chaturdashi, ten days after Chaturthi.
So why make a god from clay, feed him for days, and then give him to the water? Go back to the start of the week, to Prahlada. His furious father points at a stone pillar.
Your Vishnu is everywhere, you say?
Is he in this pillar? Yes, says the boy. The king strikes it, and out of the stone bursts Narasimha.
That's the teaching under visarjan, the way many Hindus explain it: God is everywhere already. The clay image was a seat where he was invited to sit for a while, never the whole of him.

teach.h: INVITED IN, SENT OFF: EVERY PUJA.
teach.b: Every puja has these two moments, the inviting, avahana, and the sending off, visarjana; Ganesh Chaturthi just makes them as big as a city.

teach.h: THE CLAY GOES BACK TO THE WATER.
teach.b: So nothing is lost when the clay goes under: it goes home to the water. Many families close with a short prayer that says, roughly: I don't know how to call you, or how to send you off; forgive whatever I did wrong.

teach.h: GOD STAYS WHEN THE CLAY GOES.
teach.b: One modern problem: plaster images don't dissolve, so many families have gone back to plain clay, some immersing at home in a bucket.
And look back at the week: a boy in the fire, colors in Braj, the Mother in every being, a baby holding the universe, Ganapati in the street. Five ways of loving God, kept with your hands.

how: At the end of Ganesh Chaturthi, after one and a half to ten days, many Hindus perform a final arti and carry the clay Ganesha in procession to a river, lake or the sea for visarjan, chanting Ganpati Bappa Morya; many now use plain clay or immerse at home.

o: a boat race on the river after the harvest
a feast where Ganesha's image is kept for good
Ganesha welcomed in clay, then given back to water

games.q: what's inside the goodbye — tap the pairs.
p: the last day, the biggest crowds
inviting God in, the start of every puja

the clay image was never the whole of Ganesha
like Narasimha in Prahlada's pillar, God is everywhere already. the clay was a seat for a while, and it goes back to the water.

they don't. that's why many families have gone back to plain clay, or immerse at home.

games.q: your family's Ganesha has been with you for days. the kids love him. it's the last day. what do you do?
o: keep him on a shelf so nobody's sad.
one last arti, then carry him to the water.
wrap him up and save him for next year.
games.why: one last arti, a procession, and the water. the goodbye is part of the festival, and the crowd asks him to come early next year.

practice: Picture yesterday's Ganesha. One last arti, the lamp circling his face. Carry him with the drums to the water's edge, lower him gently, and let go; watch the water close.

If you pray, say the closing prayer in your own words: I didn't know how to call you or send you off; forgive what I got wrong; come again. If you don't, say it to the year that's ending: thank you, come again.

wordCard.voice: Ganesh Chaturthi. He arrives in clay on the fourth day, stays as a guest, and is given back to the water, with a promise to come again.

orig.note: Sanskrit: letting go, release. the immersion that ends the festival.

carryVoice: Your line: visarjan. God stays when the clay goes. That's the week, and day one hundred forty-seven.
